title: Why does nine divide the reversed number take away the number?
description: {{NAME_1}} picks forty seven, reverses it to seventy four, takes the smaller from the larger and divides by nine. Letters for the two digits show the result is nine times the gap between the digits. Keeko doubts the trick and says it works only for lucky numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: write the number as ten times the tens digit plus the ones digit, subtract the reverse, and the nines group together. Watch for students who think a trick that works for one number is proved.

source: Shubham picks 47. Follow Mukta's trick, then show with lette
video_script.why: The child sees that letters for the two digits prove the trick for every two digit number, not only forty seven.
video_script.substitution: Write the number as 10a + b and its reverse as 10b + a with b larger than a, subtract, group the nines, and check with 47.
video_script.anchor: the number 47 and its reverse 74 on the board, then the same two numbers written with letters
video_script.wrong_answer: the trick only works for lucky numbers
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko sees that forty seven works and says the trick only works for lucky numbers like forty seven, so one try is taken for the whole answer.
video_script.payoff_line: Nine always divides the result, and the answer is the larger digit take away the smaller digit

final_answer.spoken: nine times bee take away eigh

names.{{NAME_1}}: the child who picks forty seven
names.{{NAME_2}}: the child who shows the reverse and subtract trick

maths_rules: 47 = 10 × 4 + 7; a number with digits a and b is 10a + b; the reverse is 10b + a; b > a
9b − 9a = 9 × (b − a), so the result is divisible by 9
slip: a trick that works for 47 is not a proof for every number
video_script.design: One idea: letters stand for any digits, so the nines group together for every number. The number and its reverse stay on the board, first as 47 and 74 and then as letters. Keeko's doubt is that the trick works only for lucky numbers.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; the number 47 written, its reverse 74, and 74 − 47 = 27, 27 ÷ 9 = 3

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.ask: the words every two digit number? appear

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is from your book. {{NAME_2}} shows {{NAME_1}} a number trick.
<bookmark mark='pick'/>{{NAME_1}} picks forty seven and reverses the digits to get seventy four.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Seventy four take away forty seven is twenty seven. Nine divides twenty seven three times, with nothing left over.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Will this happen for every two digit number with different digits?

beats.on_screen: the numbers stay on the board while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: 47 = 10 × 4 + 7; letters: tens digit a, ones digit b, number = 10a + b; the word divisible with its meaning

marks.letters: the digits become the letters a and b, and the number becomes 10a + b
marks.div: the word divisible by 9 is written with its meaning

beats.colours: tens part and ones part in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='tens'/>Forty seven is four tens and seven ones, so it is ten times four plus seven.
<bookmark mark='letters'/>Use letters now. Put eigh in the tens place and bee in the ones place. The number is ten times eigh plus bee.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Divisible by nine means nine divides it with nothing left over.

beats.on_screen: Given: a two digit number with tens digit a and ones digit b, different digits, b larger than a

marks.given: the number and its digits are written with letters

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a two digit number with eigh in the tens place and bee in the ones place. The digits are different, and bee is larger.

beats.on_screen: To show: the reverse take away the number is divisible by 9

marks.find: the aim is written on the board

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to show that nine divides the reverse take away the number.

marks.num: 10a + b is written for the number
marks.rev: 10b + a is written for the reverse

narration: <bookmark mark='num'/>Step one, write both numbers by place value. The number is ten times eigh plus bee.
<bookmark mark='rev'/>The reverse is ten times bee plus eigh.

marks.group: the b terms and the a terms are grouped

beats.colours: the b terms and the a terms in two colours
narration: <bookmark mark='take'/>Step two, take the number away from the reverse. That is ten bee plus eigh, take away ten eigh plus bee.
<bookmark mark='group'/>Group the bees and the eighs.
<bookmark mark='nines'/>Ten bee take away bee is nine bee. Eigh take away ten eigh is minus nine eigh.

marks.common: the common 9 is pulled out in front
marks.div: the words 9 divides it are written

beats.colours: the common 9 in the accent colour
narration: <bookmark mark='common'/>Step three, take out nine, because both parts have nine. Nine bee take away nine eigh is nine times bee take away eigh.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Nine is a factor of the result, so nine divides it.

beats.on_screen: Step 4, check with 47: b − a = 7 − 4 = 3 and 9 × 3 = 27
narration: <bookmark mark='gap'/>Step four, check with forty seven. Bee take away eigh is seven take away four, which is three.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>Nine times three is twenty seven, the same as before.

beats.on_screen: Answer: result = 9 × (b − a), always divisible by 9

marks.ans: the answer result = 9 × (b − a) is boxed
marks.gap: b − a glows as the digit gap

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Nine always divides the result, and the answer is the larger digit take away the smaller digit.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The result is nine times the gap between the two digits.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the numbers
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 47 only; the letters a and b slide in over it and cover every two digit number

marks.many: the whole list of two digit numbers scrolls past
marks.fix: the letters a and b cover the list

beats.colours: the wrong idea in the warning colour
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the trick only works for lucky numbers like forty seven.
<bookmark mark='many'/>There are too many two digit numbers to try one by one.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But eigh and bee stand for any digits, so the working covers every number.
